segments.title: Blackburn T.3 Velos: Greek Navy roles and seaplane design
segments.body: The Velos was a two-seat development of the Blackburn Dart and the third aircraft in the firm's torpedo-aircraft series, designated T.3. Major F. A. Bumpus designed it in 1925 around a 450-horsepower Napier Lion V engine to meet a Greek Navy requirement. Its coastal-defence brief combined torpedo dropping with reconnaissance, bombing and training. The Velos was primarily a seaplane that could receive a wheeled undercarriage when required. The Dart began as a deck-landing aircraft that could be converted into a seaplane, so the two designs approached conversion from opposite starting points.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies the Velos as a two-seat Dart development for a Greek Navy coastal-defence role and contrasts its seaplane configuration with the Dart.

segments.summary: The T.3 Velos was a two-seat Blackburn torpedo aircraft built for the Greek Navy's coastal-defence, reconnaissance, bombing, and training duties.

segments.title: Why the Blackburn Dart's reliability outweighed a sleeker shape
segments.body: Blackburn could produce a smoother, more aerodynamic aircraft, yet the Velos remained a modified Dart. Cost was one reason for retaining the older design. The Dart was already known for exceptional reliability, and customers sought that rugged dependability from Blackburn. Reliability took priority in naval aviation at the time, especially for single-engine aircraft.

evidence.note: The presenter contrasts aircraft forms, then says cost and the Dart's established reliability explain Blackburn's appeal, especially for single-engine naval aircraft.

segments.summary: Cost and the Dart's proven reliability help explain why Blackburn kept building the Velos despite being able to produce smoother aircraft.

segments.title: Greek Velos production and dual-control training aircraft
segments.body: During the second half of 1925, Blackburn took over and completed construction of Greece's National Aircraft Factory. A five-year contract put Blackburn in charge of operating it with local labour to build further Velos aircraft. Two demonstration machines had identical cockpits and dual controls. They were intended for shipment to Athens for training before delivery of the first Greek-built aircraft.

evidence.note: Blackburn completed the Greek National Aircraft Factory in the second half of 1925 and obtained a five-year contract to run it with local labour to manufacture Velos aircraft. Two dual-control demonstrators were intended for training in Athens before Greek-built deliveries.

segments.summary: Blackburn operated Greece's National Aircraft Factory under a five-year contract, and two dual-control Velos demonstrators were intended for training in Athens.

segments.title: Velos armament and single-seat torpedo sorties
segments.body: Operational Velos aircraft carried a Lewis gun on a flush-mounted Scarff ring behind the pilot for coastal-defence duties. The second cockpit had a full set of dummy controls. It was occupied only on bombing, reconnaissance or instructional sorties. With a torpedo aboard, the Velos flew as a single-seater.

evidence.note: Operational aircraft had a Lewis gun on a flush-mounted Scarff ring behind the pilot and dummy controls in the second cockpit. That cockpit was occupied for bombing, reconnaissance or instruction, while torpedo sorties were flown as a single-seater.

segments.summary: The Velos's rear cockpit was occupied for bombing, reconnaissance and instruction, while torpedo sorties used a single-seat arrangement.
